latin.461: Dices fortasse mortem esse opus Diaboli, quae tamen peccatum sequitur divina imputationis & judicii interventu: nempe, quia Diabolus causa est peccati, quod per se & natura sua meretur mortem, nec potest ei in quo, vel a quo est, nisi intercedat satisfactio, non imputari.
latin.462: At peccatum illud primum actuale Adami, cujus ipsi author serpens fuit, natura sua non merebatur omnium hominum corruptionem moralem, nec erat natura sua ejusmodi, ut salva divina justitia non posset non imputari omnibus hominibus ad illud vitium ipsis infigendum. Quod si putes tale fuisse natura, & discedes a sententia magnorum virorum qui tecum imputationem illam tuentur, & pergratum nobis feceris, si id docueris & probaveris.
latin.463: Secundum tuum Argumentum exsculpis ex Ps. 32. 1. 2. Beatus cui dimittitur praevaricatio, cui tegitur peccatum: Beatus homo cui non imputavit Dominus iniquitatem, ea arte, quam mihi mirari magis licet, quam assequi. Quis enim mentis oculus, ut ut lynceus, videre possit in illis verbis immediatam peccati actualis Adami toti posteritati imputationem? Tu tamen multis verbis efficere conaris, ut eam tecum in illis videam, sed non possum. Utinam tui argumenti vim adhibita forma syllogistica retexuisses, nec magna verborum copia obruisses; ex quibus eam eruere non possum.
latin.464: Testatur Psaltes in genere beatum esse, cui peccatum non imputatur, nempe, quod vel commisit, vel in se habet; quod autem peccatum nobis possit jure imputari, vel non imputari non docet. Probas miserum esse cui peccatum imputatur, Concedo. Addis, si hoc verum est in genere de omni peccato, verum etiam esse de peccato originali, quod in Adamo contraximus, ab Adamo dicendum fuisse videtur. Concedo hoc quoque. Subjicis, vitium illud originis esse poenam primi peccati primorum parentum; id, quoniam poenam proprie dictam intelligis, id ipsum est quod inter nos quaeritur.
latin.465: Ais nomina, quibus Psaltes peccata nuncupavit, posse primam illam Adami rebellionem significare, nempe, haud minus, quam, vel Caini homicidium, vel populi Israelitici rebellionem. Adjicis eam esse ἀνομίαν, qua voce usus est Apostolus in citando hoc loco: Esto; quid inde sequatur nondum intelligo: idem enim de Caini homicidio, de Sodomorum crimine, de Absalomi incestum & rebellione, & denique de quovis alio cujusvis scelere dicere licet. Sed tu ipse aliquid concludis, te igitur audiamus. Inde, inquis, concludere debemus secundum Apostolum verbis Prophetae utentem, illum esse beatum cui peccata non imputantur, & ex consequenti, illum esse miserum cui peccata imputantur, & cum miseria nostra tota sit a peccato primo Adami, si peccatum illud nobis imputatur, nos esse miseros, si e contra nobis non imputetur, nos esse beatos. Tu nobis, opinor, subsumendum reliquisti, Atqui non sumus beati: Ergo nobis peccatum illud imputatur.
latin.466: Taceo hujus tui argumenti materiam ob terminorum multitudinem formam syllogisticam non admittere. Taceo idem posse de quovis alio peccato dici, si nobis imputetur, nos esse miseros. Aio ut beati simus, non sufficere unius cujusdam peccati non imputationem, sed requiri omnium. Aio conferre ad meam beatitudinem, non si mihi aliquod peccatum non imputetur, puta incestus Judae, sed si mihi illud non imputetur ex gratia, quod mihi posset imputari ex justitia. Nego autem nobis primum peccatum actuale posse imputari ex justitia. Aio denique miseriam nostram totam esse a peccato primo Adami, non quia nobis proxime imputetur, sed quia causa est ejus peccati, quod quia nobis inest, ac proinde nostrum est, potest nobis imputari ex justitia.

pass_a.461: Perhaps you answer that death is the Devil's deed, yet sin comes after it through God's charging and judging: the Devil causes a sin that of itself deserves death, and that sin cannot help being charged to the one in or by whom it stands—unless satisfaction comes between.
pass_a.462: Adam's first actual deed, though the serpent authored it, did not by nature earn everyone's moral ruin, nor was it by nature such that justice could not leave it uncharged to all when fixing that vice in them. Call it such by nature and you quit the great defenders who share your imputation—and Placeus will thank you if you teach and prove it.
pass_a.463: Second you dig out of Ps. 32:1–2 the blessedness of forgiven, covered, uncharged sin—by a craft Placeus may wonder at more than catch. Even a lynx-keen mind's eye cannot spot there an immediate charging of Adam's actual deed to all offspring. You pile words to make him see it with you; he cannot. Better you had restated the force in plain syllogism than drowned it in a heap of words he cannot mine.
pass_a.464: The Psalmist testifies in general that one is blessed to whom sin is not imputed—namely what one committed or has in oneself; but he does not teach which sin may or may not rightly be imputed to us. That one to whom sin is imputed is miserable—Placeus grants. If that is true of every sin in general, it is true also of original sin contracted in Adam—granted too. You subjoin that origin's vice is the penalty of the first parents' first sin; and since you mean penalty properly so called, that is the very point in dispute between you.
pass_a.465: You say the Psalmist's names for sins can signify that first rebellion of Adam no less than Cain's murder or Israel's rebellion. You add it is anomia, the Apostle's word citing this place: granted; what follows Placeus does not yet see—the same can be said of Cain, Sodom, Absalom, or any crime. But you yourself conclude: according to the Apostle using the Prophet, blessed is he to whom sins are not imputed, miserable he to whom they are; and since our whole misery is from Adam's first sin, if that is imputed we are miserable, if not we are blessed. You left us, Placeus thinks, the unspoken minor: But we are not blessed; therefore that sin is imputed to us.
pass_a.466: Placeus passes over that the matter, for multitude of terms, does not admit syllogistic form; and that the same could be said of any other sin if imputed—we are miserable. To be blessed, non-imputation of one sin is not enough; all are required. What helps his beatitude is not that some sin (say Judas's incest) is not imputed, but that by grace is not imputed what justice could impute. He denies Adam's first actual can be imputed to us from justice. Finally our whole misery is from Adam's first sin not because it is proximately imputed to us, but because it is cause of that sin which, being in us and so ours, can be imputed from justice. Tip before the Abraham-justification proof from faith imputed.

461: You will perhaps say that death is the Devil's work, which yet sin follows by the intervention of divine imputation and judgment. Namely, because the Devil is the cause of a sin which of itself and by its nature merits death, and which cannot fail to be imputed to the one in whom, or by whom, it is, unless satisfaction intervene.
462: But that first actual sin of Adam, whose author the serpent himself was, did not by its nature merit the moral corruption of all humans, nor was it by its nature of such a kind that, divine justice being preserved, it could not but be imputed to all humans unto fixing that vice in them. And if you think it was such by nature, you will also depart from the opinion of the great men who with you defend that imputation, and you will do us a great favor if you teach and prove it.
463: Your second Argument you carve out from Ps. 32:1–2. Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered: Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed iniquity—by an art which I may admire more than follow. For what eye of the mind, however lynx-keen, could see in those words the immediate imputation of Adam's actual sin to the whole posterity? You nevertheless try with many words to make me see it with you in them, but I cannot. Would that you had rewoven the force of your argument in applied syllogistic form, and not buried it under a great abundance of words; from which I cannot dig it out.
464: The Psalmist testifies in general that one is blessed to whom sin is not imputed—namely, what one either committed or has in oneself; but which sin can rightly be imputed to us, or not imputed, he does not teach. You prove that one to whom sin is imputed is miserable: I concede. You add, if this is true in general of every sin, it is true also of original sin, which we contracted in Adam, and which seems to have had to be said from Adam. I concede this too. You subjoin that that vice of origin is the penalty of the first parents' first sin; and that, since you understand penalty properly so called, is the very thing which is in question between us.
465: You say the names by which the Psalmist called sins can signify that first rebellion of Adam, namely no less than Cain's murder, or the Israelite people's rebellion. You add that it is anomia, which word the Apostle used in citing this place: Be it so; what follows from that I do not yet understand: for the same may be said of Cain's murder, of the crime of Sodom, of Absalom's incest and rebellion, and finally of any other crime of anyone. But you yourself conclude something; let us hear you then. From there, you say, we ought to conclude according to the Apostle using the Prophet's words, that he is blessed to whom sins are not imputed, and consequently that he is miserable to whom sins are imputed, and since our whole misery is from Adam's first sin, if that sin is imputed to us, we are miserable, if on the contrary it is not imputed to us, we are blessed. You left us, I think, the minor to be subsumed: But we are not blessed: Therefore that sin is imputed to us.
466: I pass over that the matter of this argument of yours, because of the multitude of terms, does not admit syllogistic form. I pass over that the same can be said of any other sin—if it is imputed to us, we are miserable. I say that for us to be blessed, the non-imputation of some one sin is not enough, but that of all is required. I say it contributes to my beatitude not if some sin is not imputed to me—say Judas's incest—but if that is not imputed to me by grace which could be imputed to me from justice. But I deny that the first actual sin can be imputed to us from justice. I say finally that our whole misery is from Adam's first sin, not because it is proximately imputed to us, but because it is the cause of that sin which, because it is in us, and therefore is ours, can be imputed to us from justice.
